notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material from a range of commentators, but couldn't reach any Catholic, Orthodox or Lutheran site, or anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are missing (see the end). Where a source's tradition is mentioned, it comes from the source or from StudyLight's own labels.

**v. 1**
- This is a courtroom case. Ellicott calls it a lawsuit in which Jehovah is plaintiff as well as judge, and says "children of Israel" means the northern kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Ellicott says "mercy" (*chesed*) is better translated "love". It means God's covenant love for Israel and the matching love people should show to God and to each other. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Guzik: the three missing things are linked. Our understanding of who God is directly shapes our conduct. Once knowledge of God goes, truth and mercy go too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- Gill (a Baptist) says the people lived like atheists, and that this lack of saving knowledge of God was the source of all the sins that follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/4.htm
- The NET Bible note (quoted on Precept Austin) calls this a "covenant lawsuit". God, as overlord, sues his disobedient subject people for breaking the covenant, which brings on the covenant curses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "blood touches blood" means murder piled on murder. The list echoes the Ten Commandments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Gill links the bloodshed to the string of murdered kings in 2 Kings 15 (Zechariah, Shallum, Pekahiah, Pekah). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley: "break out" is like flood waters bursting over their banks, and the killings follow so closely that the end of one is the beginning of the next. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/
- Precept Austin: the Hebrew verb means breaking through barriers, pictured here as throwing off every limit God's law sets. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary

**v. 3**
- Ellicott takes the land's mourning to be famine, striking every living thing, even the fish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Gill sees the threat as sword, famine and plague. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley: God punishes man in cutting off what was made for man's benefit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hosea-4.html
- Bible.org suggests the list of animals, birds and fish may deliberately echo the creation account. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-perspectives-unfaithful-israel-hosea-41-19

**v. 4** (a hard verse with several readings)
- Guzik: the people argue with the priests God gave them to teach the Law (Deut 17:9–12), so there's no point anyone else trying to correct them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- Gill offers three readings: the people are telling the prophet not to rebuke them; God is telling the prophet to stop; or everyone is so corrupt that nobody is fit to rebuke anyone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/4.htm
- Constable: God, as judge, silences the accused in his own court. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-4.html
- Ellicott records a different reading from the Speaker's Commentary. A small change in the Hebrew vowel marks gives "And thy people, O priest, are as my adversaries." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Matthew Henry draws a lesson: as long as there is hope, we owe it to each other to rebuke sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hsa/Hsa_004.cfm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: the priest works by day and the prophet dreams by night, and both will fall. "Your mother" means the nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley: "your mother" is both the kingdom and its places of worship. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/
- Precept Austin takes these to be false prophets who said judgment would never come. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik: the people had some knowledge, just not enough. What they lacked was knowledge of God and of his Word. Pastors who fail to preach the Word will answer to God for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- Ellicott: the priests should have kept this knowledge alive among the people. If the people themselves are being addressed, the verse means Israel loses its calling to be a priestly nation (Exod 19:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Gill (Calvinist Baptist) makes a point you won't find in the others. He says the verse cannot mean the elect, God's people by special grace, since they can never be finally destroyed. It means Israel as a nation, God's people in name only. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley: the knowledge meant is of God, his law, his providence, his holy nature, his hatred of sin and power to punish it. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/
- Precept Austin: "rejected knowledge" runs parallel to "forgotten the law". The people didn't just lack knowledge, they actively turned it down. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary
- The NET Bible translates the verse "You have destroyed my people by failing to acknowledge me!" https://biblehub.com/lexicon/hosea/4-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: God gave the priests growth, but blessing brings more accountability, and they sinned all the more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- Wesley applies it to kings, priests and people: Sin grew with their wealth and honour. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/
- Constable: "their glory" means their large population, or perhaps Yahweh Himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-4.html

**v. 8**
- Wesley, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Ellicott all take "sin" to mean the sin offerings, part of which went to the priests. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/4-8.html
- Benson (a Methodist): the priests were glad to see the people sin, because more sin meant more offerings for them to eat. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/4-8.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik gives two senses. The priests won't escape judgment. And priests come from the people, so a backslidden people produces backslidden priests. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- The Pulpit Commentary applies the same principle to the final judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-4.html

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: the punishment fits the sin. Feeding on the people's sins leaves the priests hungry, and their sexual sin leaves them childless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Constable: God will send drought and lower their fertility. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-4.html
- Precept Austin: the sins they thought would bring prosperity brought emptiness instead. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: "heart" means the whole inner life. Wesley: these things rob people of understanding and judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm; https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/
- The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics calls this a great moral truth about all sin, and especially sins of the body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/hosea/4.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: the "wood" is idols carved from wood. The early church father Cyril took the "staff" to be fortune-telling with rods. It might instead be the idol itself, since the goddess Asherah was worshipped as a wooden pole. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley reads the "spirit of prostitution" as both spiritual and physical. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/
- Guzik: Israel wanted to add other gods alongside the LORD, which is like adultery against a faithful husband. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: hilltops were the usual sites for idol shrines ("high places"). The trees named are white poplar and terebinth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Precept Austin: the pleasant shade shows how comfort can hide spiritual corruption. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary

**v. 14** (readings really differ here)
- Ellicott: God won't punish the women because they are more sinned against than sinning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Guzik: God has no double standard in sexual morality. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- Precept Austin: the women aren't innocent. They just won't be singled out, because the men are equally or more guilty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary
- Wesley reads it as a judgment, not leniency: I will give them up to their own hearts. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: Judah is warned not to copy Israel. Gilgal and Beth-aven were centres of idol worship. "Beth-aven" ("house of wickedness") is a mocking twist on Bethel ("house of God"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- Ellicott notes that one ancient Greek manuscript reads "On" (Heliopolis in Egypt, a centre of sun worship). Some have suggested Jeroboam got his calf worship from there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley: Judah must not mix the worship of God (here, swearing by his name) with idol worship. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/

**v. 16**
- Guzik: if you act like a stubborn cow, don't expect to be protected like an obedient sheep. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
- Ellicott: the German scholar Ewald read the lamb image as tender pity. Most commentators read it as a threat: a lamb left alone and exposed in the wilderness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley sides with the threat reading: a wilderness with no rest, safety or food. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/

**v. 17** (much preached; the split runs across traditions, not between them)
- Who is told to "leave him alone"? Ellicott: Judah. He adds that the Jewish scholars Rashi and Kimchi took it as God telling the prophet to stop. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- **God gives the sinner up:**
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) preached it as God's response when people keep on sinning after being warned. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/let-him-alone/
  - Guzik: All God must do to make certain a man goes to hell is simply let him alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-4/
  - Wesley and Clarke (Methodists) both call Ephraim beyond reclaiming. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/4-17.html
- **Keep away from him:** MacLaren says the verse does not license doubting the gospel's power. It calls the church to keep separate from an idolatrous world. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/hosea/let-him-alone.cfm
- **Pastoral comfort:** William Jay (quoted in the Biblical Illustrator): if you can't let God alone, that proves he hasn't let you alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/4-17.html
- The NET Bible translates it "Do not go near him!" https://biblehub.com/hosea/4-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Ellicott says the King James wording here is poor. He reads "her shields love shame", with "shields" meaning the rulers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/4.htm
- Wesley: their wine is spoiled, and "give ye" points to bribery and oppression. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/

**v. 19**
- Wesley: The whirlwind of wrath from God hath seized this old adulteress. What they trusted in will become their shame. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-hosea/
- Precept Austin: a picture of sudden judgment and exile, the nation swept away like chaff in a storm. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-4-commentary

**What's missing**
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I didn't reach newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Lutheran and Reformed sites:** I found nothing from lcms.org, 1517.org, ligonier.org or thegospelcoalition.org.
- **Modern scholarship:** Bibleodyssey.org had nothing. The only NET Bible material came second-hand: one note quoted on Precept Austin, plus its translations of v. 6 and v. 17.
- **Prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace:** I found no discussion of how these teachings use the chapter, including the popular use of v. 6.
- **Partial pages:** The pages for Gill (after v. 9), Enduring Word (after v. 15) and Precept Austin (after v. 1) were cut off when I opened them. My notes on their later verses come only from search-result excerpts.
